title: The Helpful Caller: Social Engineering at the Fleet Console
summary: A caller posing as vendor support, and a former contractor's account that was never closed, open a way into the fleet management system.

decision_points.context: Shortly before the morning departure bank, the shift lead gets a call from someone who says they are from the vehicle vendor's support team. They say a critical update must go out before the bank and ask the shift lead to turn on remote access to the fleet console and read back the one-time access code.

options.text: Turn on remote access and read the code, since the update sounds urgent.
Refuse, hang up, and carry on with the shift.
Refuse, call the vendor back on the number in the support contract, and report the call to security.
Turn on remote access but watch the session closely.

decision_points.context: Security reviews fleet console sign-ins after the call. They find that the account of a maintenance contractor whose contract ended three weeks ago signed in late last night.
decision_points.prompt: How do you handle the account?

options.text: Disable the account now, preserve the sign-in records, and review what it accessed.
Disable the account and move on.
Leave the account active and email the contractor's former manager to ask about it.
Reset the password but keep the account in case the contractor comes back.

decision_points.context: The review shows no changes were made to the vehicles, but the account could see fleet routes and schedules. Leadership asks what should change.

options.text: Send a reminder email about phishing to all staff.
Role-based social-engineering training for ramp and operations staff, least-privilege console roles, and an offboarding step that closes accounts when contracts end.
Ban all vendor remote access permanently.
No change, since nothing was damaged.
